Okay, Uber might have been a “ little bit of a crapshoot ” for riders looking to book a robotaxi, per Waymo’s co-CEO. Yes, notching just four ride bookings via AI agents during the Halloween period probably wasn’t the spooky season performance it had hoped for. And alright, the company’s president defecting to OpenAI might have added to what hasn’t, on the surface, been a great news week for Uber. Park all of that for just a minute, however, and some of the numbers out of Uber’s third-quarter report earlier this week must still have been enough for execs still at the company to cheer at least a little. Although revaluing equity investments weighed on earnings to the point of missing, Uber revenues rose 9.6% from last year to hit $14.77 billion and beat estimates. Trips taken on Uber — that is, slightly confusingly, the sum of trips taken in Uber cars and total deliveries made on Uber Eats — hit a staggering 4.06 billion in the quarter. That tally means that each of Uber’s 215 million monthly active platform users must have ordered a taxi, or a taxi for their burrito , just shy of 19 times (more than six times each month) on average last quarter. Imagine how many more the company could’ve clocked without the driver shortages in India, Canada, and Brazil that it also disclosed this quarter . For those of you who see that trip figure and still assume Uber mostly functions as a ride-hailing service, the company’s split on gross bookings, which rose 20% from last year to reach almost $60 billion in the third quarter, might not be what you expect… and the balance might not have been how you thought for a while now. Since Delivery gross bookings value overtook Mobility during the pandemic era — remember? Not many of us were taking taxis and a lot of us were getting stuff delivered because there was nothing else to do? — there’s really not been a huge margin separating the two in either direction. In the last quarter, Uber booked $29.5 billion from rides and just around $1 billion less from its Delivery segment; its Freight division, which brought in $1.8 billion, still clearly has a ways to go. While some of the more eye-catching Uber news this week might not have looked great on paper, the billions of trips and hundreds of millions of riders and users that the company notches each quarter undoubtedly softened the blow. title: 🌊 The blue wave washed data centers away
body_text: Sweetgreen is in a tough spot. The premium-priced slop bowl seller has recently been caught in a vortex of rising labor costs, increasing wholesale food prices, and choppy sales. The company is eager to be known as something other than the place that sells $20+ salads. Instead, the Wall Street Journal reports that Sweetgreen is eager to be known as the place with the $15 wraps. The company is also beefing up portion sizes and making build-your-own salad pricing more transparent in an effort to woo customers. Perhaps the only people more dejected by Tuesday’s election results than Republican politicians are data center developers. Data centers – the kilowatt-sucking warehouses filled with server racks and cooling equipment – were on the ballot across the country and the results were emphatic: Voters don’t like data centers. They really really don’t like data centers. In the 41 local races across the country where a data center moratorium, new regulations, or a specific project itself was on the ballot, voters weighed in against data centers 40 times, Semafor reports . Those election night results don’t come out of the blue, of course. Back in May, Gallup found that 71% of Americans opposed data center construction in their area. To put that 71% opposition figure in context, building new data centers is just about as unpopular as releasing the Epstein files is popular ( 75% of Americans support the latter.) In terms of the market reaction to voters’ data center displeasure, it would be easy to look at the post election rally in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 and think that meant that investors expected little to no hiccups in the AI trade, and specifically, the data center trade, to proceed with little to no hiccups while Democrats control the House and Senate. Looking a bit more granularly at the market reaction, that doesn’t seem to be the case. While the broad indices are indeed up, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF and the RoundHill Memory ETF – which as their names indicate, respectively track semiconductor and memory storage shares – ended the day in the red. Nvidia , Broadcom , and Marvell all tumbled. (In a sign of just how negative investor sentiment is, AMD printed strong earnings and boosted guidance and ended the day barely eking out a gain.) And who among the AI trade gained on the day? The hyperscalers – Amazon , Google , Meta , Microsoft – were all in the green. SpaceX was conspicuously down, as investors reassessed the downsides of Elon Musk’s close alliance with the President Trump and the failure of Musk’s interventions on behalf of the GOP in Texas’s statewide races. What investors are saying, in a sense, is that if right now you have an already operating data center, it just got more valuable . And if your business is selling stuff to build not-yet-existing data centers, that business just got on balance a little less profitable going forward. As Bloomberg’s Joe Weisenthal put it , the “[Meta Hyperion] campus in Louisiana might be able to charge some pretty high rents.” The massive data center build out in recent years across the Sun Belt in particular was done in large part with full industry enmeshment with the national and state Republican party. That strategy will now largely be unavailable. However, in a purely analytical way – dare we mention game theory ? – despite the tables being fully turned, that strategy had a certain logic. Indeed, if you were in charge of a hyperscaler or an AI lab with an interest in seeing data centers getting built, being as close as possible to Trump and the GOP may have made sense. Assuming a blue wave was coming and there was nothing really that you could do about it, Trump and the GOP were the path to getting the most compute online while you could. Any data center that wasn’t already up and running on Monday has a lower chance of becoming operational and a longer lead time with higher costs if it does. The challenge that the entire data center and AI industry must now reckon with is the blue wave did indeed happen, and Democrats will (accurately!) view their anti-data center campaign messaging as key in helping them win. An industry not used to oversight or much, if any, national-level regulation will now be a key regulatory and investigation target of a party emboldened by a historic win. In response, OpenAI has already decided to rebrand data centers as “ compute campuses .” I’d hazard to predict that won’t be enough to turn the anti-data center tide. 🏈TNF: The Jacksonville Jaguars are a surprise favorite in a Thursday night matchup against the Baltimore Ravens, thanks largely to the likely season-ending thumb injury of Baltimore’s star quarterback Lamar Jackson on Sunday. body_text: Judges ruled that McDonald’s must defend a lawsuit over claims that its popular McRib — which has morphed into a bit of a sales panic button for the fast-food giant in recent years — has been misleading customers for years, given that it doesn’t actually contain meat cut from the ribcage, but “ seasoned boneless pork dipped in a tangy BBQ sauce .” The plaintiffs are presumably in for another rough day when someone finally decides to burst the bubble on bacon bits and crab sticks as well… Stocks finished Tuesday slightly up but mostly flat as markets awaited the midterm results. When you think of the company that Steve Jobs founded some 50 years ago , your mind likely first arrives at the various devices that have truly revolutionized the way we live in the modern world, of which the company now says there are 2.5 billion in active use globally. However, Apple’s Services division — often the source of those just-small-enough-to-dismiss transactions that leave your account each month, with various cloud and content subscription payments tacked on to give users the full run of Apple’s walled garden — has become a huge part of the pie, with revenues reaching yet another record in the company’s fourth quarter. In Q4, sales from Services reached a whopping $31.57 billion, up some 9.8% from the same period last year. While that might have snapped a double-digit growth streak that had run for 12 quarters in a row, as analysts quoted by Variety observed, it still means that Apple offerings such as TV+, Music, Pay, Podcasts, News+, and others are raking in more than $13 billion more each quarter than they were five years ago. The difference between how much profit Services takes in compared to Apple’s main cash cow, the Products segment, also speaks for itself: The cost of sales on the whopping $82.9 billion that Products brought in for Q4 was $52.1 billion, while the Services segment's cost of sales for the same period was just $7.6 billion. While slowing growth and the unending popularity of Apple’s devices — the company this week said it’s unsure whether it will be able to get more iPhone Duos in by the all-important Christmas trading period, after the $2,000 foldables sold out in a matter of weeks — might mean Services will never catch up to Products in the amount of cash they generate for the company, the profit race between the two has been getting more interesting.
